newsitem.title: USA: Defense seeks separate trials in Oklahoma bombing.
newsitem.headline: Defense seeks separate trials in Oklahoma bombing.

text.p: If the two defendants in the Oklahoma City bombing case were tried together it would be too difficult for juries to be fair to both men, defence experts testified Wednesday in a pre-trial hearing.

Lawyers for defendants Timothy McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols asked U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch to sever the trials, arguing the evidence to be used against each defendant was sufficiently different to warrant separate hearings.
It would be too difficult for juries to apply such evidence to only one defendants, the defence teams said.
Matsch set aside three days for the hearing, which began Wednesday.
Prosecutors were seeking the death penalty for McVeigh and Nichols, accused of the 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, which claimed 168 lives.
Prosecutors said two trials would be more expensive and time-consuming than one and the only way to paint a complete picture of the crime for the jury would be to try both men together.
Matsch was expected to rule within several weeks on the motion to separate the trials.
Prosecutors argued that if any evidence should only be applied to one defendant it can be done so through the judge's instructions to the jury.
Outside the courtroom McVeigh's attorney Stephen Jones told reporters that statements Nichols made two days after the bombing include 68 references to McVeigh.
"How many times do you instruct (the jury) - 68 times?" he asked. The statements were not made public.
Prosecutor Sean Connelly told reporters that in the 10th U.S. District Court, which covers Colorado, case law showed that instructions to the jury could remedy such problems.

Attorney Bryan Stevenson and a retired criminal appeals judge from Texas, Charles Campbell, testified that the problem becomes acute during the penalty phase of a trial after defendants are convicted.

Stevenson heads the Southern Centre for Human Rights, a non-profit group that represents defendants in capital cases. He testified that in the penalty phase a defence attorney must get the jury to focus on the life of the convicted man and that becomes harder when two people are tried together.
"They're fighting against one another to put themselves in the best light," Campbell testified.
Under cross-examination Stevenson said he opposed the death penalty.
Prosecutors also said they wanted to spare victims and relatives of victims the pain of going through two trials. Cost was another factors.

Separately, prosecutors filed with the court an affidavit from a paralegal who conducted a computer search on death penalty cases and found that for jointly tried defendants, 60 percent received life imprisonment while 40 percent got the death penalty.
In cases where defendants were tried separately, 62.5 percent received the death penalty and 37.5 percent got life terms.
Connelly told reporters the study showed defendants could receive a fair hearing when tried together.
The trial was moved to Denver becauses of widespread publicity and strong feelings in Oklahoma. It was expected to get under way early next year, although no date was set.
